title: SYSK Live in Nashville: The Biosphere II Experiment
summary: Live recording at the Schermerhorn Symphony Center in Nashville, Tennessee of Stuff You Should Know covering the Biosphere 2 experiment. The hosts trace its roots to John Allen's Synergia group (Synergians) in 1960s San Francisco, their move to the Synergia Ranch in New Mexico, and their ship Heraclitus. They explain the project's goal of a sealed, self-sustaining habitat for studying biospherics and Mars-habitat research, funded by billionaire Ed Bass. They describe the eight biospherians who sealed in on September 26, 1991, the five biomes, the design flaws (unsealed biomes, weak lashed trees, ocean turning to algae, concrete carbon sink), hunger and food shortages, the breathing crisis and oxygen injection, the press and scientific backlash, Ed Bass's takeover with Steve Bannon as CEO, the breaking of the seal in 1993, and the project's lasting scientific legacy and current University of Arizona operation. The episode is a live show with a lot of banter and some ads; the hosts also mention the trip to Oracle, Arizona.

segments.title: Live show opening in Nashville
segments.summary: Hosts greet the live audience at the Schermerhorn Symphony Center in Nashville and mention their January research trip to Oracle, Arizona.

segments.title: What Biosphere 2 was
segments.summary: Hosts frame Biosphere 2 as a sealed attempt to replicate Earth and introduce the idea that the group was not a cult.

segments.title: John Allen and the Synergians in 1960s San Francisco
segments.summary: John Allen, nicknamed Johnny Dolphin, gathers a creative group in San Francisco that stages performance art as the Theater of All Possibilities and tours as the Caravan of Dreams. They move to New Mexico and form Synergia Ranch.

segments.title: Research vessel Heraclitus and the project's origins
segments.summary: The Synergians build the research ship Heraclitus from scratch. The hosts explain the biosphere idea, which grew from concern about Earth's ecosystems and the new field of biospherics.

segments.title: Lab versus field science and the project's purpose
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the tradeoff between lab and field studies and how a compact biosphere could speed up carbon cycle studies and serve as a testbed for Mars habitation. Linda Lee's small-jungle idea is mentioned.

segments.title: Ed Bass funding and the business plan
segments.summary: Billionaire Ed Bass, son of Texas oil tycoon Perry Bass, funds the project at roughly 150 to 200 million dollars. The plan includes patentable research and charging tourists admission through Space Biosphere Ventures.

segments.title: Architecture and original one-hundred-year plan
segments.summary: The architect Phil Hawes designs the facility with aluminum tubing and a geodesic dome. The original plan was a 100-year sealed experiment with rotating crews.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Message break with sponsor reads.

segments.title: Return from break and sealing in
segments.summary: Hosts return and note the start of the mission on September 26, 1991.

segments.title: The eight biospherians
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the eight crew members, including Mark Nelson, Abigail Alling, Jane Poynter, Roy Walford, Mark van Thillo, Sally Silverstone, Taber MacCallum and Linda Lee. Poynter leaves briefly after a rice huller accident and returns with duffel bags.

segments.title: Crew relationships and roles
segments.summary: The hosts describe the crew's roles, the couples within the group, and Sally Silverstone as the cook.

segments.title: Biomes, species and the human wing
segments.summary: The facility has five biomes, including a rainforest with a waterfall, savannah, coastal fog desert, freshwater and mangrove marshes, and a 700,000-gallon ocean, plus a purple human wing and a farm. About 3,800 species were introduced.

segments.title: Facility size and life inside
segments.summary: The three-acre facility is compared to a Sears at Rivergate Mall. Life inside is described as isolated, with visitors paying to watch the crew.

segments.title: Design flaws
segments.summary: The biomes were not sealed from one another, and the hosts describe the flaws in the design and the lack of realistic science because of this.

segments.title: Desert turning to scrub, algae ocean and lashed trees
segments.summary: Excess moisture from the rainforest turned the desert to scrub, the ocean became choked with algae from nutrients, and trees grew weak without wind and had to be lashed to the dome.

segments.title: Species loss, invasive ants and pollination
segments.summary: The biosphere lost about 40 percent of species, better than predicted. Morning glory and crazy ants thrived, and crops had to be hand-pollinated. A bush baby died in an electrical panel.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Message break with sponsor reads.

segments.title: Hunger and the farm
segments.summary: Calorie counts fell well short of plans as the crew farmed and got hungry. Roy Walford's calorie-restricted diet results showed weight loss and improved blood markers.

segments.title: Food shortages and coffee
segments.summary: The hosts describe the crew's diet of sweet potatoes, beets, bananas and goat milk, and a coffee shortage that limited each person to a few cups.

segments.title: Factions and tension
segments.summary: Crew members split into factions over John Allen's authority, and tension grew, including Abigail Alling saying she was spat at.

segments.title: Oxygen decline and CO2 problem
segments.summary: Oxygen fell and CO2 rose to the equivalent of high altitude, caused by rich soil microbes and a concrete carbon sink. The team considered leaving or pumping in oxygen and chose to pump oxygen.

segments.title: Undisclosed scrubber and press backlash
segments.summary: The media first praised the project and then turned on it. Undisclosed CO2 scrubbers and the duffel bags added to the backlash, and scientists distanced themselves.

segments.title: PR failure and end of the first mission
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the failure of public relations, with the crew denying problems. The crew emerged on September 23, 1993.

segments.title: Mission two, Biodome and Ed Bass's takeover
segments.summary: The second mission had three crew members. Ed Bass staged a takeover, John Allen was removed, and Steve Bannon became CEO.

segments.title: Breaking the seal
segments.summary: Mark van Thillo and Abigail Alling broke the seal to the facility to protect the crew from the new direction.

segments.title: Legacy and University of Arizona
segments.summary: The facility is no longer closed. The hosts discuss research that came from the project, including wastewater treatment and coral bleaching from ocean acidification. The University of Arizona now runs it.

segments.title: Environmental legacy and visiting
segments.summary: The hosts reflect on the project's effect on environmentalism and mention the bush babies' reproduction and visiting tips.

segments.title: Tucson restaurant recommendation and ghost story
segments.summary: The hosts recommend a restaurant in Tucson and share a ghost legend about the bush babies at the facility.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Nashville and close the episode.
